research_period: Shows 10 September to 6 October 2026; Premiere Vision Paris, February 2026; analysis October to November 2026
markets: Global: New York, London, Milan, Paris and Copenhagen runways; applies to premium and mid-market womenswear
title: SS27 Women's Woven Silhouette Direction
summary: The skirt replaces the loose trouser as the anchor of the spring wardrobe. Straight and pencil skirts at knee to mid-calf, the dropped-waist dress and the short, waisted jacket lead; bubble volume is a styling moment rather than a volume buy.

sections.heading: The evidence
sections.body:
The clearest signal of the season is measurable. Across 12,320 SS27 womenswear looks, skirts rose from 19.3% to 27.9% of looks against SS26, while dresses fell from 37.0% to 33.3%<sup>[1]</sup>. The fastest-rising key item was the straight skirt, which doubled from 5.1% to 10.3%; the dropped-waist dress grew from 0.6% to 4.9%<sup>[1]</sup>. On the other side of the ledger, loose trousers fell from 11.5% to 3.0% of looks, chinos from 6.7% to 1.5% and mini dresses from 9.8% to 4.8%<sup>[1]</sup>.

The shows explain the numbers. Prada put a skirt in every look, treating it, in the house's words, as "this unique and universal garment"<sup>[2]</sup><sup>[3]</sup>. Chanel cut narrow skirts to just below the knee, the length Gabrielle Chanel considered most flattering<sup>[2]</sup>, in smocked tweed and sheer organza<sup>[3]</sup>. At Dior, Jonathan Anderson ran the full range, from gauze-light minis to ankle-length, flared, pleated and tulle-trimmed skirts<sup>[4]</sup>. Across Milan and Paris the dominant lengths were knee and mid-calf<sup>[4]</sup>.

Retail buyers read it the same way. Elodie Abrial, commercial director of the Le Bon Marché group, described skirts with "a great deal of fluidity and movement"<sup>[2]</sup>. Victoria Dartigues, director of womenswear buying at Galeries Lafayette Paris, linked the season's move to separates to wardrobes that "encourage self-creation rather than adopting a uniform"<sup>[2]</sup>.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body:
The shift is structural rather than decorative. Designers rebuilt the season around separates: Daniel Roseberry at Schiaparelli said the house reinvented its dresses and necklines "as tops and bottoms"<sup>[2]</sup>. A wardrobe built from separates sells in more combinations, which is why department stores are framing it as a buying opportunity rather than a runway story.

It also follows two seasons of very relaxed trousers. With loose trousers and chinos falling sharply in runway share<sup>[1]</sup>, the skirt takes the role of the easy, comfortable bottom, and tailored trousers hold steady at 12.4% of looks<sup>[1]</sup>. Heat is the third driver: designers were explicit that the collections answered Europe's summer temperatures with lighter, single-layer clothes<sup>[3]</sup>.

sections.heading: Shapes to lead with
sections.body:
**Straight and pencil skirt, knee to mid-calf.** The volume driver of the season. Straight and pencil shapes led in Milan<sup>[5]</sup>; Saint Laurent paired gold pencil skirts with trench coats<sup>[5]</sup>. Build it as a core shape in suiting, satin and denim.

**The full, layered midi skirt.** Dior, Chanel and the Australian label Aje showed long, light, layered skirts<sup>[5]</sup>; Prada used layered crinolines, organza shells and tulle<sup>[4]</sup>. Commercially, this works best in two or three layers of light cloth rather than structured petticoats.

**The dropped-waist dress.** Back on the runway<sup>[5]</sup> and among the fastest risers<sup>[1]</sup>. Pair the dropped seam with a pleated or flared skirt; keep the bodice relaxed.

**The short, waisted jacket.** Cropped jackets replaced oversized shapes at Jil Sander, Tod's and Marni, while Armani, Gucci and Jil Sander cinched jackets at the waist<sup>[4]</sup>. Oversized blazers were scarce in Milan<sup>[5]</sup>. Givenchy showed cinched peplum tailoring<sup>[3]</sup>.

**Bias-cut slips and 1930s gowns.** Chanel's collection included bias-cut 1930s gowns<sup>[4]</sup>; satin slips carry the same line into day wear.

sections.heading: Shapes to handle with care
sections.body:
**The pouf and bubble skirt.** Christian Lacroix's mid-1980s shape returned at Loewe and Dior, in very short versions at Miu Miu and Zimmermann, and as a denim sculpture at Comme des Garçons<sup>[2]</sup>. FashionUnited's report notes the trend may fade quickly because the pieces are more image-driven than wearable and are almost impossible to sit in<sup>[2]</sup>. Forecut's assessment: use bubble hems for editorial and occasion pieces, not for core volume.

**Micro hems and the mini dress.** Etro, Roberto Cavalli and Gucci showed micro hems<sup>[4]</sup>, but the mini dress halved its share of looks<sup>[1]</sup>. Keep minis as a small, younger-customer option.

**Very loose trousers and chinos.** The sharpest fallers of the season<sup>[1]</sup>. Reduce depth and move the customer to a straight, tailored trouser; a relaxed straight leg is replacing the curved barrel jean in denim<sup>[5]</sup>.

timing: In stores February to July 2027. The straight skirt and the waisted jacket are rising now; Forecut expects both to carry into AW27 in heavier cloth. The bubble skirt is likely to peak within SS27 itself and should not be carried forward in depth. The dropped-waist dress is at an early stage: test in SS27, build in SS28 if sell-through supports it.
products:
- **Skirts:** straight and pencil skirts at knee and mid-calf; pleated and layered midi skirts; satin slip skirts; denim midi skirts.
- **Dresses:** dropped-waist dresses with pleated skirts; bias-cut slip dresses; long column dresses for evening.
- **Jackets:** cropped, waisted jackets; one-button cinched jackets; peplum jackets.
- **Customers:** the core is the working woman who buys separates and builds a wardrobe over seasons, the customer Galeries Lafayette describes. Younger customers will pick up the bubble hem and the mini in small doses.
design_implications:
- **Set the lengths first.** Plan skirts at three lengths: just below the knee, mid-calf and ankle. The knee and mid-calf lengths carry the volume<sup>[4]</sup>.
- **Engineer movement.** Narrow knee-length skirts need a walking vent, kick pleat or slit; check stride and sitting in the first fitting.
- **Waist placement matters again.** Jackets stop at the natural waist or are belted there; dropped-waist dresses move the seam to the hip. Avoid long, unshaped blazers.
- **Finish carries the price.** Waistbands, linings and hems decide quality in a skirt; fit depends on waist and hip grading, and bias-cut styles should hang before hemming<sup>[5]</sup>.
- **Build in pairs.** Design skirts and jackets to work together and apart, reflecting the season's separates logic<sup>[2]</sup>.
commercial_implications:
- **Move budget from trousers to skirts.** With loose trousers and chinos falling sharply<sup>[1]</sup>, shift part of the trouser buy into straight and midi skirts while holding a tailored trouser as the core.
- **Expect better multi-buys.** Separates encourage customers to buy two or three pieces that work together; plan coordinated skirt and jacket stories in shared colours.
- **Cap the bubble skirt.** Treat it as a short-run fashion piece with a clear exit date<sup>[2]</sup>.
- **Reduce mini dresses** in favour of midi and maxi lengths; maxi dresses held a 16.0% share of looks<sup>[1]</sup>.
- **Price ladder:** core straight skirts at entry and mid price in suiting and denim; layered organza and satin midi skirts at a premium.
